issues.legal_issue: Amounts forfeited after failed negotiations to sell a capital asset retain their capital character rather than becoming revenue receipts.
material_facts: The company grew rubber and tea but did not carry on the business of selling trees.
It agreed to sell old, unyielding rubber trees, which were capital assets, and received earnest money and advances from the purchasers.
The purchasers failed to pay the balances, the agreements ended, and the company retained the amounts under their terms.
The retained sums related directly to the proposed sale of the trees; had the sales been completed, the consideration would have been capital and potentially subject to capital gains tax.
issues.conclusion: The forfeited earnest money and advances were capital receipts, not revenue receipts assessable as income from the company’s business or other sources.
issues.legal_principle: The capital or revenue character of a receipt is determined by the nature of the transaction and the asset to which it relates; the cancellation of a sale of a capital asset does not change the character of money received in negotiations for that sale. The Court relied on Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, Kerala v. Kailas Rubber & Co. Ltd. (1966) 60 ITR 435 and AKTM Vishnudatta Anantharjanam v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, Trivandrum (1970) 78 ITR 58 for the capital character of proceeds from old, unyielding rubber trees. It applied Morley (Inspector of Taxes) v. Tattersall (1939) 7 ITR 316, while noting from Commissioner of Income Tax v. Karam Chand Thapar [1996] 10 SCC 577 that a subsequent event can sometimes imprint a different quality on a receipt; cancellation of a capital-asset sale did not do so here. The contractual forfeiture operated as compensation for breach under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, as considered in Maula Bux v. Union of India, AIR 1970 SC 1955 and Shree Hanuman Cotton Mills v. Tata Air Craft Ltd., AIR 1970 SC 1986. Under the rule stated in London and Thames Haven Oil Wharves Ltd. v. Attwooll (Inspector of Taxes) (1968) 70 ITR 460, compensation for failure to receive a sum is treated as that sum would have been treated; the amounts promised here would have been capital receipts.

rule.if: income_tax_receipt_character_case and capital_asset_sale_negotiations and purchaser_default_ended_sale_agreement and seller_retained_negotiation_money and contract_allowed_retention_on_breach and not asset_held_for_sale_business

predicates.income_tax_receipt_character_case: The proceeding concerned the income-tax character of a receipt.
predicates.capital_asset_sale_negotiations: The seller negotiated to sell an asset held as a capital asset.
predicates.purchaser_default_ended_sale_agreement: The purchaser’s default caused the proposed sale agreement to end.
predicates.seller_retained_negotiation_money: The seller kept money received in connection with the proposed sale.
predicates.contract_allowed_retention_on_breach: The agreement provided for the seller to retain the money following the purchaser’s breach.
predicates.asset_held_for_sale_business: The seller held the asset as part of a business of selling such assets.

issues.definition: When an income-tax receipt-character case concerns money retained after a purchaser’s default ended negotiations to sell a capital asset, and the seller did not hold the asset for a selling business, the retained amount is treated as capital rather than revenue if the agreement allowed its retention on breach.

issues.legal_issue: Forfeited earnest money retained from negotiations to transfer a capital asset is included among the advance or other money addressed in the capital-gains cost computation rule.
material_facts: The company received both earnest money and advances under agreements to sell old rubber trees that were capital assets.
After the purchasers defaulted and the agreements ended, the company retained both kinds of payment.
On remand, the Tribunal treated the forfeited advances as non-revenue receipts but treated the earnest money as income.
The agreements concerned negotiations for the transfer of the trees, which were eventually sold to another purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The earnest money, like the advances, fell within the rule for money received and retained in respect of negotiations to transfer a capital asset; the distinction between earnest money and advances did not exclude the earnest money.
issues.legal_principle: Section 51 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 provides that, when a capital asset is transferred, advance or other money received and retained in respect of an earlier occasion of negotiations for its transfer is deducted from the asset’s cost, written-down value, or fair market value, as applicable, in computing cost of acquisition. The words “or other money” include earnest money, so the provision makes no relevant distinction between earnest money and an advance. The Court held that this treatment preserves the rule in Morley (Inspector of Taxes) v. Tattersall (1939) 7 ITR 316.

rule.if: capital_gains_cost_computation_case and capital_asset_was_transferred and prior_transfer_negotiations_occurred and seller_received_and_retained_negotiation_money

predicates.capital_gains_cost_computation_case: The proceeding concerned computing the capital gain on a transferred asset.
predicates.capital_asset_was_transferred: The owner transferred an asset held as a capital asset.
predicates.prior_transfer_negotiations_occurred: Before the transfer, the owner had negotiated to transfer the asset.
predicates.seller_received_and_retained_negotiation: The owner received and kept money in respect of those earlier negotiations, including money paid as earnest money or an advance.

issues.definition: When a capital asset is transferred after earlier negotiations and the owner received and retained money relating to those negotiations, that money reduces the asset’s cost for capital-gains computation.
